guides.hardware: Any GPU with 4GB+ VRAM, or a CPU with 8GB+ RAM (slower but fine)
guides.title: Train a Tiny Language Model, End to End
guides.objective: Train a ~0.8M-parameter character-level transformer on Tiny Shakespeare from scratch, sample text from it, and learn to read a loss curve. Every command is copy-pasteable; every step tells you what success looks like.

blocks.label: train.py — training loop

checks: Smoke test finishes in minutes with no errors and prints falling loss
Full run prints lines like: step 0: train 4.18 | val 4.19 ... step 1800: train ~2.1 | val ~2.3
Ends with saved tiny.pt
steps.expected: Loss starts near ln(65) ≈ 4.17 (random guessing over 65 chars) and falls toward roughly ~2.1 train / ~2.3 val. Exact numbers vary with hardware and seed — the shape (fast drop, then slow grind, val slightly above train) is what matters. CPU takes on the order of an hour; a GPU takes minutes.

fixes.fix: See the Fix common failures step. First test: overfit one batch (batch_size = 1, train on it) — loss must hit ~0. If it does not, the loop has a bug.
Drop learning_rate to 3e-5 and rerun. If it persists, a bad batch snuck in — re-download input.txt.
Halve batch_size (32 -> 16 -> 8) and block_size (128 -> 64). This model fits almost anywhere, so OOM means something else allocated the GPU.

steps.title: Sample from the model

checks: You can state your final train loss, val loss, and perplexity
Val loss is a bit above train loss (small gap = healthy; huge gap = overfitting)
You logged tokens/sec or step time at least once
steps.expected: Perplexity around ~10 means: at each position the model is as confused as if choosing among ~10 equally likely characters — down from 65 at random. Compare runs by val loss, never by train loss.

fixes.fix: Normal at this scale — the model memorized 1MB of text. Regularize (dropout 0.1, weight_decay 0.01) or, better, move to a bigger corpus in the 10M project.
fixes.s: Val loss much higher than train loss

steps.goal: Turn your loss numbers into a judgment: did it work, and how do you know?
steps.title: Evaluate like an engineer

checks: You can match each symptom below to its fix without re-reading
steps.expected: Four failure modes cover ~90% of tiny-run pain. The overfit-one-batch test is the single most useful debugging habit in deep learning.

fixes.fix: Overfit one batch first (batch_size = 1). If loss hits ~0, the loop is correct and the model just needs more steps, more LR (try 1e-3), or more capacity. If it cannot overfit one batch, the bug is in data or loss.
Cut learning_rate 10x (3e-4 -> 3e-5). Rerun. NaN almost always means the step size exploded the weights, not broken data.
batch_size 32 -> 8, block_size 128 -> 64. If still OOM on GPU, something else is holding memory (nvidia-smi to check).
This is expected on CPU (roughly an hour for 2000 steps). Smoke-test at 200 steps while editing, then launch the full run and walk away. GPU? Minutes.
